claim: Background selection and GC-biased gene conversion together affect as much as 95% of the variants of the human genome.
source: Here, we use high-quality human genomic data to show that purifying selection at linked sites (i.e. background selection, BGS) and GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) together affect as much as 95% of the variants of our genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of genomic data showing the pervasive effects of BGS and gBGC across the genome, as demonstrated in the results section.

claim: The magnitude and relative importance of BGS and gBGC are largely determined by variation in recombination rate and base composition.
source: We find that the magnitude and relative importance of BGS and gBGC are largely determined by variation in recombination rate and base composition.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing relationships between recombination rate, base composition (WS, SW, WW+SS sites), and the effects of BGS and gBGC as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Synonymous sites are affected by BGS and gBGC.
source: Importantly, synonymous sites and non-transcribed regions are also affected, albeit to different degrees.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis showing that synonymous sites show different SFS patterns compared to neutral sites, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Non-transcribed regions are affected by BGS and gBGC.
source: Importantly, synonymous sites and non-transcribed regions are also affected, albeit to different degrees.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B showing that DAFi increases with recombination rate even in non-transcribed regions more than 50 kb away from transcribed regions.

claim: The use of synonymous sites and non-transcribed regions for demographic inference can lead to strong biases.
source: Their use for demographic inference can lead to strong biases.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Figure 3 showing markedly different demographic parameters inferred from synonymous sites, NTR-50kb sites, and neutral sites.

claim: SNPs with recombination rates above 1.5 cM/Mb and mutation types C↔G, A↔T (WW+SS sites) are mostly unaffected by BGS or gBGC.
source: However, by conditioning on genomic regions with recombination rates above 1.5 cM/Mb and mutation types (C↔G, A↔T), we identify a set of SNPs that is mostly unaffected by BGS or gBGC, and that avoids these biases in the reconstruction of human history.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C showing that DAFi reaches a plateau above 1.5 cM/Mb for WW+SS sites, indicating minimal effect of BGS and gBGC.

claim: Various measures of diversity are positively correlated with levels of recombination in humans.
source: In humans, various measures of diversity are positively correlated with levels of recombination (Nachman, 2001; Spencer et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2009; Lohmueller et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that have documented this correlation.

claim: A direct mutagenic effect of recombination seems unlikely except at CpG sites.
source: While a direct mutagenic effect of recombination seems unlikely (McVicker et al., 2009; Schaibley et al., 2013) except at CpG sites (Arbeithuber et al., 2015), there is still some debate about whether the correlation between diversity and recombination is driven by recurrent selective sweeps (hitchhiking of neutral and slightly deleterious mutations) or background selection (BGS; i.e. purifying selection against deleterious mutations at linked sites) (McVicker et al., 2009; Stephan, 2010; Hernandez et al., 2011; Lohmueller et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that have investigated the mutagenic effect of recombination.

claim: The modeling of genomic diversity under selection in humans suggests that it can be explained entirely by BGS.
source: The modeling of genomic diversity under selection in humans suggests that it can be explained entirely by BGS (Lohmueller et al., 2011), whereas a combination of both BGS and positive selection seems to best explain genomic diversity in Drosophila (Elyashiv et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lohmueller et al., 2011.

claim: A combination of both BGS and positive selection seems to best explain genomic diversity in Drosophila.
source: The modeling of genomic diversity under selection in humans suggests that it can be explained entirely by BGS (Lohmueller et al., 2011), whereas a combination of both BGS and positive selection seems to best explain genomic diversity in Drosophila (Elyashiv et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Elyashiv et al., 2016.

claim: The correlation between diversity and recombination is generally relatively weak in humans for most tested statistics and seems restricted to genomic regions of relatively low-recombination rate (<1 cM/Mb).
source: However, the correlation between diversity and recombination is generally relatively weak in humans for most tested statistics and seems restricted to genomic regions of relatively low-recombination rate (<1 cM/Mb, (Cai et al., 2009; Lohmueller et al., 2011)).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2009 and Lohmueller et al., 2011.

claim: GC-biased gene conversion is a process by which GC alleles in recombination tracts are preferentially transmitted in GC/AT heterozygotes.
source: However, regions of high recombination might be prone to GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC), a process by which GC alleles in recombination tracts are preferentially transmitted in GC/AT heterozygotes (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Duret and Galtier, 2009, which describes the mechanism of gBGC.

claim: gBGC increases the frequency of G and C derived alleles relative to A and T, especially in recombination hotspots.
source: This process thus increases the frequency of G and C derived alleles (usually denoted as strong or S alleles, Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014) relative to A and T (denoted as weak or W alleles), especially in recombination hotspots (Spencer et al., 2006; Glémin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spencer et al., 2006 and Glémin et al., 2015.

claim: gBGC affects the site frequency spectrum such that it becomes right-shifted for W-to-S mutations and left-shifted for S-to-W mutations.
source: By modifying allele frequencies in high-recombination regions, gBGC affects the site frequency spectrum (SFS) (Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014; Glémin et al., 2015) such that it becomes right-shifted for W-to-S (WS) mutations and left-shifted for S-to-W (SW) mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014 and Glémin et al., 2015, and is also demonstrated in Figure 2B.

claim: WS SNPs show larger levels of population differentiation than other SNPs.
source: In addition, gBGC affects various classical statistics used to detect selection, and WS SNPs show larger levels of population differentiation than other SNPs (Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014.

claim: gBGC is believed to directly affect only 1% to 2% of the human genome, near recombination hotspots.
source: Overall, gBGC is believed to directly affect only 1% to 2% of the human genome, near recombination hotspots (Glémin et al., 2015), but due to the transient nature of these hotspots, a larger fraction of the genome could have been affected in the long term.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Glémin et al., 2015.

claim: Due to the transient nature of recombination hotspots, a larger fraction of the genome could have been affected by gBGC in the long term.
source: Overall, gBGC is believed to directly affect only 1% to 2% of the human genome, near recombination hotspots (Glémin et al., 2015), but due to the transient nature of these hotspots, a larger fraction of the genome could have been affected in the long term.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the transient nature of hotspots.

claim: Southern and Eastern Asians show a slight yet significant deficit in the number of derived alleles compared to the three other groups.
source: The number of derived alleles is indeed broadly comparable across individuals from different geographic regions, even though Southern and Eastern Asians (SAS and EAS) show a slight yet significant deficit in the number of derived alleles than the three other groups (~50,000 out of 17 million, Tukey test, p<0.01) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting either a more efficient selection, a lower mutation rate or a longer generation time.
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing (Tukey test, p<0.01) and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: BGS is clearly acting in non-transcribed regions even when focusing on regions more than 50 kb away from any transcribed region.
source: Interestingly, BGS is clearly acting in NTR regions even when we focus on NTR regions more than 50 kb away from any transcribed region (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1B showing the effect of recombination rate on DAFi in NTR-50kb regions.

claim: BGS in non-transcribed regions could be due to the presence of functional elements such as non-coding RNAs, histone marks, enhancers or insulators.
source: This result confirms that BGS is acting in NTRs (Asthana et al., 2007; Comeron, 2014; Rands et al., 2014), which could be either due to the presence of functional elements in these regions such as non-coding RNAs, histone marks, enhancers or insulators (Kellis et al., 2014; Bonev and Cavalli, 2016; Van Nostrand et al., 2017), or due to remote effects of exonic deleterious mutations on SNPs in NTR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying functional elements in non-coding regions.

claim: Filtering by GERP score may not be sufficient to completely remove the effect of BGS.
source: These observations suggest that filtering by GERP score may not be sufficient to completely remove the effect of BGS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that even sites with neutral GERP scores show a relationship with recombination rate.

claim: BGS should have a minimal influence in regions of high recombination.
source: Since the impact of BGS is mediated by recombination, BGS should have a minimal influence in regions of high recombination (Hudson and Kaplan, 1995; Nordborg et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hudson and Kaplan, 1995 and Nordborg et al., 1996, and is consistent with theoretical expectations.

claim: GC biased gene conversion is acting in GC/AT heterozygotes in regions of high recombination, particularly in the vicinity of recombination hotspots.
source: However, it has been shown that GC biased gene conversion (gBGC) is acting in GC/AT heterozygotes in these regions, particularly in the vicinity of recombination hotspots (Spencer et al., 2006), potentially increasing the frequency of G and C derived alleles (usually denoted as strong or S alleles, see Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014) as compared to A and T (denoted as weak or W alleles).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spencer et al., 2006 and Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014.

claim: The non-monotonic behavior at SW sites is consistent with gBGC favoring the transmission of G and C alleles.
source: This non-monotonic behavior at SW sites is consistent with gBGC favoring the transmission of G and C alleles, and thus decreasing the frequency of derived A and T alleles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern and the known mechanism of gBGC.

claim: SNPs located in regions where recombination is higher than 1.5 cM/Mb are affected by gBGC and not by BGS.
source: These results suggest that SNPs located in regions where recombination is higher than 1.5 cM/Mb are affected by gBGC and not by BGS (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6C).
evidence: This is inferred from the patterns observed in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 6C.

claim: WW and SS sites with a recombination rate above 1.5 cM/Mb represent 2.88% and 2.94% of all SNPs for 1000G and SGDP datasets, respectively.
source: Therefore, WW and SS sites with a recombination rate above 1.5 cM/Mb (representing 2.88% and 2.94% of all SNPs for 1000G and SGDP datasets, respectively) should be optimal for demographic inference, as they appear to evolve mainly neutrally.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: WW and SS sites with a recombination rate above 1.5 cM/Mb should be optimal for demographic inference, as they appear to evolve mainly neutrally.
source: Therefore, WW and SS sites with a recombination rate above 1.5 cM/Mb (representing 2.88% and 2.94% of all SNPs for 1000G and SGDP datasets, respectively) should be optimal for demographic inference, as they appear to evolve mainly neutrally.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these sites show a plateau in DAFi and are not affected by gBGC.

claim: BGS affects the SFS in complex ways.
source: BGS thus affects the SFS (Zeng and Charlesworth, 2011) in complex ways (Nicolaisen and Desai, 2013), and the comparison of sites that are differentially exposed to BGS allows us to better examine this influence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zeng and Charlesworth, 2011 and Nicolaisen and Desai, 2013.

claim: The SFS computed in ten 1000G populations for different recombination classes shows distortions that are qualitatively similar in all populations.
source: The SFS computed in ten 1000G populations for different recombination classes (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) shows distortions that are qualitatively similar in all populations, irrespective of differences in demographic history.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing similar SFS patterns across populations.

claim: The second-to-lowest recombination class shows an excess of singletons and a deficit of intermediate and high frequency variants compared to the highest recombination class.
source: As compared to the highest recombination class, the second-to-lowest recombination class (which is potentially the one most strongly affected by BGS) not only shows an excess of singletons, but also a deficit of intermediate and high frequency variants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A showing the SFS for different recombination classes.

claim: The difference between the SFSs of unbiased mutations (WW + SS) and biased mutations (SW and WS) increases with recombination rate.
source: In line with previous work (Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014), we find that the difference between the SFSs of unbiased mutations (WW + SS) and biased mutations (SW and WS) increases with recombination rate.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B and is consistent with previous work by Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014.

claim: WS mutations show a deficit of low-frequency variants and an excess of intermediate- and high-frequency variants in regions of high recombination.
source: In particular, WS mutations show a deficit of low-frequency variants and an excess of intermediate- and high-frequency variants in regions of high recombination (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B showing the SFS for WS mutations in different recombination classes.

claim: The excess of high-frequency variants at WS sites is not compensated by a corresponding deficit of high-frequency variants at SW sites.
source: As previously recognized (Katzman et al., 2011; Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014), the excess of high-frequency variants at WS sites is not compensated by a corresponding deficit of high-frequency variants at SW sites, implying that gBGC could contribute to the increase of nearly fixed derived alleles that has previously been attributed to mislabelled ancestral states or positive selection (Hernandez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B and is consistent with previous observations by Katzman et al., 2011 and Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014.

claim: gBGC could contribute to the increase of nearly fixed derived alleles that has previously been attributed to mislabelled ancestral states or positive selection.
source: As previously recognized (Katzman et al., 2011; Lachance and Tishkoff, 2014), the excess of high-frequency variants at WS sites is not compensated by a corresponding deficit of high-frequency variants at SW sites, implying that gBGC could contribute to the increase of nearly fixed derived alleles that has previously been attributed to mislabelled ancestral states or positive selection (Hernandez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed excess of high-frequency WS variants.

claim: The SFS observed at synonymous sites differs markedly from that observed at neutral sites.
source: Interestingly, the SFS observed at synonymous sites differs markedly from that observed at neutral sites, as it comparatively shows a significant deficit of low-frequency variants and a large excess of high-frequency variants (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing the comparison of SFS at synonymous and neutral sites.

claim: The excess of high-frequency variants at synonymous sites is due to gBGC.
source: It appears that this latter excess is due to gBGC, as it disappears when one computes the SFS on synonymous sites not affected by gBGC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing that the excess disappears when SW and WS sites are removed from synonymous sites.

claim: Very different demographies can be inferred from neutral and non-neutral SFSs.
source: Our results thus clearly show that very different demographies can be inferred from neutral and non-neutral SFSs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing markedly different demographic parameters inferred from different SFS datasets.

claim: BGS and gBGC affect the SFS of populations with distinct histories in a qualitatively similar way.
source: However, even though BGS and gBGC affect the SFS of populations with distinct histories in a qualitatively similar way, they have different consequences on their reconstructed demography.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different populations show similar SFS distortions but different demographic inferences.

claim: It appears difficult to predict how demographic parameters will be biased when using non-neutral SFS.
source: It thus appears difficult to predict how demographic parameters will be biased when using non-neutral SFS.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different populations show different biases in demographic inference.

claim: Simulated BGS patterns qualitatively match the observations very well.
source: Overall, the simulated BGS patterns qualitatively match the observation very well (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing simulated and observed patterns in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: Up to 80–85% of the human genome is probably affected by background selection.
source: Here, we show that up to 80–85% of the human genome is probably affected by background selection (BGS), an effect that is not subtle (Reed et al., 2005) and that is visible from single individuals genomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of DAFi patterns across the genome and is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The estimate of the fraction of the human genome influenced by BGS matches relatively well with that reported to be biochemically functional by the ENCODE consortium.
source: Even though our estimate of the fraction of the human genome influenced by BGS matches relatively well with that reported to be biochemically functional by the ENCODE consortium (Bernstein et al., 2012), our results do not imply that 80–85% of the human genome is functional.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous estimates from the ENCODE consortium.

claim: The results do not imply that 80–85% of the human genome is functional.
source: Even though our estimate of the fraction of the human genome influenced by BGS matches relatively well with that reported to be biochemically functional by the ENCODE consortium (Bernstein et al., 2012), our results do not imply that 80–85% of the human genome is functional.
evidence: This is an explicit clarification of the interpretation of the results.

claim: Functional sites that are the direct target of purifying selection in both coding and non-coding regions potentially represent 8–15% of the genome.
source: They rather show that functional sites that are the direct target of purifying selection in both coding and non-coding regions (potentially representing 8–15% of the genome, Rands et al. (2014); Graur, 2017) have an important but indirect influence on most of the genome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rands et al., 2014 and Graur, 2017.

claim: Functional sites under purifying selection have an important but indirect influence on most of the genome.
source: They rather show that functional sites that are the direct target of purifying selection in both coding and non-coding regions (potentially representing 8–15% of the genome, Rands et al. (2014); Graur, 2017) have an important but indirect influence on most of the genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BGS affects a much larger fraction of the genome than the fraction under direct selection.

claim: The effect of BGS extends well beyond coding regions in humans.
source: As expected, the effect of BGS is clearly mediated by local recombination rate, but it extends well beyond coding regions in humans (Hernandez et al., 2011) (Figure 1), and it is thus not restricted to species with a large effective size (Corbett-Detig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1 and is consistent with previous work by Hernandez et al., 2011.

claim: BGS is not restricted to species with a large effective size.
source: As expected, the effect of BGS is clearly mediated by local recombination rate, but it extends well beyond coding regions in humans (Hernandez et al., 2011) (Figure 1), and it is thus not restricted to species with a large effective size (Corbett-Detig et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of BGS effects in humans, which have a relatively small effective population size.

claim: The influence of gBGC is not restricted to recombination hotspots.
source: Our results also show that the influence of gBGC is not restricted to recombination hotspots (Spencer et al., 2006; Glémin et al., 2015), but that it has also a strong footprint in regions with a recombination rate larger than 1.5 cM/Mb, but note that it could affect (to a lesser degree) regions with an even lower recombination rate (see Figure 1—figure supplement 5D.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1C showing gBGC effects in regions with recombination rate above 1.5 cM/Mb.

claim: Regions with recombination rate larger than 1.5 cM/Mb represent about 15.9% and 16.2% of the polymorphic positions for the 1000G and SGDP datasets, respectively.
source: These regions represent about 15.9% and 16.2% of the polymorphic positions for the 1000G and SGDP datasets, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis.

claim: BGS and gBGC together affect more than 95% of the polymorphic sites in the human genome.
source: Taken together, BGS and gBGC thus affect more than 95% of the polymorphic sites in our genome, and we have identified only a small fraction of all genomic SNPs (~3%, Supplementary file 2 - Table S2) that can be considered as evolving neutrally.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined effects of BGS (affecting 80-85%) and gBGC (affecting ~16%).

claim: Only a small fraction of all genomic SNPs (~3%) can be considered as evolving neutrally.
source: Taken together, BGS and gBGC thus affect more than 95% of the polymorphic sites in our genome, and we have identified only a small fraction of all genomic SNPs (~3%, Supplementary file 2 - Table S2) that can be considered as evolving neutrally.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the data analysis reported in Supplementary file 2 - Table S2.

claim: Neutral SNPs are found in both transcribed and non-transcribed regions.
source: Interestingly, our neutral SNPs are found in both transcribed and non-transcribed-regions (Figure 2C), and they are enriched close to telomeric regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 10), where BGS is predicted to be weaker (Charlesworth, 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing similar SFS for TR and NTR regions in the neutral set.

claim: Neutral SNPs are enriched close to telomeric regions, where BGS is predicted to be weaker.
source: Interestingly, our neutral SNPs are found in both transcribed and non-transcribed-regions (Figure 2C), and they are enriched close to telomeric regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 10), where BGS is predicted to be weaker (Charlesworth, 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 10 and is consistent with theoretical predictions by Charlesworth, 2012.

claim: Recombination hotspots still play a role in decoupling selected from neutral sites within the neutral set.
source: It thus seems that recombination hotspots still play a role in decoupling selected from neutral sites, and that sites furthest away from hotspots might still be slightly sensitive to BGS.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of DAFi as a function of distance to hotspots shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9B.

claim: Sites furthest away from recombination hotspots might still be slightly sensitive to BGS.
source: It thus seems that recombination hotspots still play a role in decoupling selected from neutral sites, and that sites furthest away from hotspots might still be slightly sensitive to BGS.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative relationship between DAFi and distance to hotspots shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9B.

claim: BGS and gBGC can have different impacts on the inferred demography of populations.
source: However, we show that BGS and gBGC can have different impacts on the inferred demography of the populations.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing different demographic biases for Yoruba and Japanese populations.

claim: BGS and gBGC lead to an underestimation of the age of a bottleneck and an overestimation of the magnitude of a demographic expansion in the Yoruba population.
source: For instance, we found that they lead to an underestimation of the age of a bottleneck and an overestimation of the magnitude of a demographic expansion in the Yoruba population, but we do not observe such strong biases in the Japanese population.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing the demographic inferences for the Yoruba population.

claim: Future studies of demographic history should be based on a set of markers that is minimally influenced by non-neutral forces.
source: We therefore suggest that future studies of demographic history should be based on a set of markers that is minimally influenced by these non-neutral forces.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The removal of exonic SNPs and those located close to phastCons elements from the neutral set would have no major effect on the shape of the SFS.
source: In conclusion, even though exonic SNPs and those located close (≤0.0003 cM) to phastCons elements show different SFS shapes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), their removal from our neutral set would have no major effect on the shape of the SFS, since they represent only a small fraction (2.2% and 16.9% respectively) of the SNPs in our neutral set.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of SFS for different subsets of the neutral set.

claim: Filtering out SW and WS SNPs from regions with B > 0.9 may result in a good alternative data set for demographic inferences.
source: We suspect that the main discrepancy with our neutral set is the presence of gBGC in regions with B > 0.9, such that filtering out SW and WS SNPs may result in a good alternative data set on which to perform demographic inferences
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the analysis of different neutral sets.

claim: Methods of demographic inference based on whole genomes should be sensitive to BGS and gBGC.
source: Methods of demographic inference based on whole genomes (e.g. Li and Durbin, 2009; Sheehan et al., 2013; Schiffels and Durbin, 2014) should also be sensitive to BGS and gBGC, since they assume that heterozygosity levels within individuals is not driven by local recombination rates nor selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the assumption that these methods make about heterozygosity levels.

claim: The history of human populations might be more readily inferred from methods that can analyze restricted sets of neutrally evolving sites interspersed across the genome.
source: In this respect, the history of human populations as well as that of other species might be more readily inferred from methods that can conveniently analyze restricted sets of neutrally evolving sites interspersed across the genome.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Other types of inference using a biased neutral SFS as a reference could also be affected, such as inferences of the distributions of fitness effects.
source: Similarly, other types of inference using a biased neutral SFS as a reference could also be affected, such as inferences of the distributions of fitness effects (DFE) (Keightley and Eyre-Walker, 2010; Kim et al., 2017; Tataru et al., 2017), even though the magnitude of the effect remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential impact on other types of inference.

claim: The approach can be readily applied to any species for which a recombination map is available.
source: Due to its simplicity, our approach can be readily applied to any species for which a recombination map is available.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: The expected number of derived mutations is the same for any individual in the sample across its whole genome, irrespective of the particular demography of its population, assuming neutrality.
source: We show in the Materials and methods below how this statistic depends on the average time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) of the whole sample, and, if one assumes neutrality that this statistic should be the same on expectation for any individual in the sample across its whole genome, irrespective of the particular demography of its population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated theoretically in the Materials and methods section and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in the number of derived alleles among individuals and among genomic regions should reflect differences in selection, mutation rate and/or generation time.
source: Differences in the number of derived alleles (ni) among individuals and among genomic regions should therefore only reflect differences in selection, mutation rate and/or generation time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical derivation showing that demography should not affect DAFi under neutrality.

claim: The use of alternative recombination maps leads to similar patterns of DAFi vs recombination rate.
source: Local recombination rates around each SNP were obtained from the 1000G Yoruba recombination map (Frazer et al., 2007) (see Materials and methods), but the use of alternative recombination maps leads to similar patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing similar patterns with different recombination maps.

claim: The same log-linear relationship between DAFi and recombination rate is observed in the SGDP dataset.
source: We observe the same log-linear relationship in a set of 20 individuals chosen to represent five continents that were sequenced as part of the Simons Genome Diversity Project (Mallick et al., 2016) at higher coverage (31–60×) than the 1000G individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A showing the relationship for SGDP data.

claim: The very similar behavior of DAFi among individuals and populations is not in line with a differential action of positive selection in different continents.
source: Note that this very similar behavior among individuals and populations is not in line with a differential action of positive selection (selective sweeps) in different continents.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all populations show similar patterns.

claim: If adaptive events were involved in shaping allele frequencies, they should have occurred before the human lineage split into different continental groups.
source: Therefore, if adaptive events were involved in shaping allele frequencies and creating this relation, they should have occurred before the human lineage split into different continental groups.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all populations show similar patterns.

claim: Most variation in exonic regions has emerged in the last 10,000 years.
source: Since most variation in exonic regions has emerged in the last 10,000 years (Fu et al., 2013), a pure adaptive explanation for this relation seems unlikely.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fu et al., 2013.

claim: A pure adaptive explanation for the relationship between DAFi and recombination rate seems unlikely.
source: Since most variation in exonic regions has emerged in the last 10,000 years (Fu et al., 2013), a pure adaptive explanation for this relation seems unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of variation emergence and the similarity of patterns across populations.

claim: A correlation between mutation and recombination rates could occur if these rates were both affected by the same process, such as replication timing or transcription rate.
source: Alternatively, a correlation between mutation and recombination rates could occur if these rates were both affected by the same process, such as replication timing (Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2009; Koren et al., 2012) or transcription rate (Gerton et al., 2000; Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on replication timing and transcription rate.

claim: Mutation rate should have no effect on the shape of the SFS.
source: Second, we find a significant difference in the shape of SFS computed in regions of low and high recombination (Figure 2A), even though mutation rate should have no effect on the shape of the SFS.
evidence: This is based on theoretical expectations about the effect of mutation rate on the SFS.

claim: The B-statistics inferred by McVicker et al. are significantly better fitted as a function of the recombination rate if we assume a log-log linear relationship between recombination and deleterious mutation rate than if we impose a constant mutation rate across the genome.
source: We find that the B-statistics inferred by McVicker et al. (2009) are significantly better fitted as a function of the recombination rate if we assume a log-log linear relationship between recombination and deleterious mutation rate than if we impose a constant mutation rate across the genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 8 showing the fit of different models to B-statistics.

claim: Under the log-log linear model, both the observed and predicted B-statistics reach a plateau value of ~0.9 above a recombination rate of ~1.5 cM/Mb.
source: Interestingly, under our log-log linear model, both the observed and predicted B-statistics reach a plateau value of ~0.9 above a recombination rate of ~1.5 cM/Mb.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 8 showing the plateau in B-statistics.

claim: In addition to BGS and gBGC, some correlation between mutation and recombination rate is required to best explain the observed patterns.

claim: Positive selection should lead to an increase of both low- and high-frequency variants in the SFS.
